description: Hi, we are the hackstreet bros, a team of high school students passionate about engineering, coding, and solving real-world problems. We have experience with Python, JavaScript, and Arduino, and we have lots of experience with building various kinds of projects whether hardware or software.
summary:
Gravitron is a browser game about designing a satellite mission, told across two generations of one family. In Story 1, set in 1958, you play Austin, a NASA engineer building one of America's first satellites. The rival company Iron Eclipse is racing to control Earth observation, so Austin must prove that satellite data can serve the public. This guided tutorial has you choose an orbit, instruments and a rocket to measure radiation around Earth and take the first weather pictures, and shows how the satellite's systems depend on each other. In Story 2, set today, Austin's grandson Ajay runs a small aerospace business funded by loans. He picks a modern mission, tracking wildfires or mapping Arctic sea ice, and wants to restore his reputation with an affordable satellite that does what the first mission could not. He has less money and less guidance, and must balance mass, power, budget and data before launch. The mission runs on real NASA wildfire data and NSIDC sea-ice data. It ends with a debrief that explains the results and what to change.
Gravitron answers the challenge by teaching players to set the goal before choosing the hardware. Its message is that useful Earth observations can be affordable, and that failed missions still leave lessons worth learning from.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

GRAVITRON is a game about designing a satellite mission under hard limits. Every flight is one loop: pick a science job, one of three orbits, parts (41 in seven groups) and one of seven rockets; pass a go or no-go review; fly month by month through events that ask for a decision; read a debrief that names the one thing that limited the flight and one change to try.

There are three modes. Part 1 is a guided 1958 walkthrough: Austin Albert builds a first satellite in three steps. Part 2 is his grandson Ajay's comeback: fly contracts to clear a debt before a deadline, with loans, a credit score from 300 to 850, rockets that can fail, a buyout offer and seven endings. Quick mode is one scored flight. Easy, Normal and Hard hide answers, never facts; on Normal and Hard the player pays engineers for information about a part.

HOW IT WORKS

Eight formulas (rocket equation, orbital period, solar power, eclipse, battery size, image resolution, data budget, margins) decide whether a design can fly. The mission runs month by month on the real records listed under NASA Data. It is one web page: no install, no account. It plays offline from a data snapshot stored in the game; online, three public feeds add a "right now" line to the debrief.

BENEFITS (IMPACT)

Anyone with a browser can learn why a spacecraft is a chain of trade-offs: each part fixes one problem and creates the next. The debrief ties the result to a real problem and to one of 14 real missions.

WHAT IS NEW (CREATIVITY)

History is part of the game: Part 1 flies the parts and rockets of 1958. In Part 2, money is the teacher: margins become cash, interest and a deadline. Two visiting satellite engineers told us the slowest part sets the schedule, so the game names it (the long pole) and shows every part's lead time. All pictures are drawn by code and all sound is made in the browser.

WHY IT IS SOUND (VALIDITY)

Part figures come from NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology State of the Art report, CubeSat 101 and NSSDCA records; anything else is labelled ESTIMATE or GAME VALUE in the data files. Prices, interest, the credit score and lead times are game values. A fire detection is one hot pixel, not one fire. More than 800 automated checks pass, including hand-worked tests of the formulas (by yarmee.)https://gitlab.com/hackstreet-bros/gravitron

NASA DATA AT THE CORE (RELEVANCE)

The NASA FIRMS files for 2025 hold 3,693,555 MODIS fire detections; a low orbit can see 92% of them, a polar orbit all, one geostationary slot 69%. The sea-ice debrief uses the NSIDC Sea Ice Index: 4.75 million square kilometres in September 2025, 26% below the 1981 to 2010 average. SILSO sunspot numbers and the Canadian Space Agency's Alouette-1 soundings drive two more topics.

THE STORY (PRESENTATION)

A notebook connects the parts: Austin writes it in 1958, Ajay opens it decades later. Screens carry few words and the debrief leads with the verdict.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

Players who can say why a mission worked or failed. Players who really engage themselves with what best practices they can discover/follow to get what they want to achieve. Next: the global leaderboard and the 1v1 duel are built and tested to encourage competition; they need a server and switch off by themselves when the game runs locally.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework, no build step (Canvas, Web Audio API, browser storage); Node.js for the tests and the optional server; Python for the script that builds the data snapshot; Git and GitLab; an SI coding assistant (see Use of SI).

EONET, Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker (wildfires, sea and lake ice)
